HASHEM’S ARMY DIVISIONS

Hashem’s army also has divisions. Four, to be exact. Can you remember where the Torah describes the Yidden as being divided into four?

Let’s go back in time. The shevatim had gone down to Mitzrayim, and their father, Yaakov, was about to pass away. “Promise me that I won’t be buried in Mitzrayim!” he instructed, “Instead, bring my body to Me’aras Hamachpeila in Chevron.” Then, he told his twelve sons how to carry his aron when the time comes: “You should travel as four divisions. Each division should be made up of three shevatim and hold a different side of my aron. Yehudah, Yissachar, and Zevulun, you will hold the eastern side of the aron. Reuven, Shimon, and Gad, you will carry the southern side. Efraim, Menashe, and Binyamin, you’ll be on the west, and Dan, Asher, and Naftali you’ll go on the north.” And so it was; the shevatim faithfully did as their father instructed.

Fast forward almost 200 years. The Jewish nation—Tzivos Hashem—now numbered in the millions, and it was finally time for them to leave Mitzrayim. How did they travel and camp throughout the midbar? It was all done in groups of shevatim, the very same way that they carried Yaakov Avinu’s aron! There were four divisions, one on each side of the mishkan, and the same three shevatim were placed on each side. This time, however, instead of each shevet being one person, they numbered tens of thousands!

So how did the crowds know where to be? To help them, each shevet had its own flag and each division had its own flag— totalling 12 shevet flags and 4 division flags. Each shevet’s flag displayed a unique color and symbol from the Torah, and each division flag had one of the following symbols: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle. When you saw your flag, you knew that you were in the right place!

EVERY ARMY DIVISIONS

Every army has different divisions. For example: the ground forces battle on land, the air force fights from the skies, the navy takes control of the seas, and the intelligence collects information about the enemy.

They all work together to win the war!

Tishrei is around the corner… which means it’s time for the exclusive Tzivos Hashem Lulav & Esrog Campaign! In last year’s Hachayol (#620), we read about Reb Yisroel Jacobson, a devoted Lubavitcher chassid who brought Yanover esrogim to America, a mission that led to the z’chus of supplying the Frierdiker Rebbe and the Rebbe with a personal esrog and lulav each year, as well as the healing of a family member. His family continues this special mission today, making these esrogim available for everyone.

Hello Chayolim! My name is Rabbi Leibel Altein, as we enter the 100th year of bringing Yanover esrogim to America, I want to share a special story about my zeide, Reb Yisroel Jacobson, and the esrogim he brought for the Rebbeim.

When the Frierdiker Rebbe arrived in America in (1940), my zeide had the privilege of supplying him with Yanover esrogim for Yom Tov. Yanover esrogim, which come from Italy, are a specific type of esrog that Chabad chassidim are careful to use. My zeide had the honor of importing and selecting the esrogim to present to the Frierdiker Rebbe and Rebbe.

Then, during the 1950s, Rabbi Mordechai Perlov, a Lubavitcher rov in Milan, informed the Rebbe that a serious issue had developed.

Until then, the esrogim in Italy had grown in wild fields. But as demand increased, local farmers realized that esrogim had become valuable and began planting their own orchards. In order to strengthen the delicate fruit, they grafted esrog trees with lemon or orange trees. Grafting involves attaching a branch from one type of tree onto another until they grow together. Once grafted, the fruit is no longer considered a kosher esrog.

Esrog Agents

The story of the Yanover esrogim - part II

At first, my father, Reb Mordechai Altein, traveled with my zeide to Italy to help with the inspections. The work was difficult. Esrogim grow on thorny bushes, and they would crawl underneath them, digging down to the roots to make sure there was no evidence of grafting.

instructed my zeide that he could no longer rely on others. He had to travel personally to Italy and inspect every tree to ensure no grafting had taken place. The Rebbe also instructed that there should be two people to witness the cutting of the esrogim so they could testify that the trees were kosher.

Several years later, in (1959) questioning how people could fully trust my zeide, since he also owned the business. The Rebbe answered by quoting —one witness is believed regarding matters of kashrus and issur. Traveling to Italy in those years was extremely expensive, and my zeide was not wealthy. The Rebbe therefore told him that he wanted to become a shutaf, a partner, in the business. Every summer, the Rebbe would give him five one-hundred-dollar bills and one single dollar bill to help cover expenses. This continued every year until (1991).

my grandfather was a mashpia in Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim and someone the Rebbe personally knew well. “He is someone people can trust.” That settled the issue.

In the early 1960s, my father was no longer able to travel with my grandfather. The Rebbe therefore instructed Rabbi Moshe Lazar, a shliach living in Milan, to join him in cutting the esrogim. Rabbi Lazar later described many times how carefully they performed this work together.

This arrangement continued until 1969, when my zeide suffered a severe heart attack and doctors told him he could no longer fly. My father then took over the responsibility and continued working with Rabbi Lazar every year.

Along with the esrogim, our family also brought lulovim to the Rebbe. My brother-in- law, Reb Yitzchok Meir Gurary of Montreal, would spend days searching through Manhattan wholesalers to find the finest lulovim for the Rebbe.

Then, in 1976, my father also suffered a heart attack and could no longer travel to Italy. The Rebbe instructed another Milan shliach, Reb Shmuel Rodal A”H, to join Rabbi Lazar instead. From then on, the two shluchim selected and cut the esrogim for the Rebbe each year.

Knowing that the Rebbe preferred larger esrogim, they carefully set aside especially beautiful ones in designated boxes.

Even though the Rebbe was technically a partner in the business, he always paid for his esrogim himself using one-hundred-dollar bills. At first he bought only esrogim that were needed for his personal use, but later he also purchased esrogim for head shluchim around the world. In later years, he would buy about fifteen to seventeen esrogim altogether. Because of this, my father collected many one-hundred-dollar bills from the Rebbe and would occasionally distribute them to his grandchildren.

know exactly why the change occurred. One year, my father noticed that the first thing the Rebbe did was separate the esrogim with pittums from those without. The Rebbe then personally chose one with a pittum for himself.

After the selections were completed, my father would often have yechidus with the Rebbe for about half an hour. They discussed family matters, including concerns about my brother, who was very ill at the time, as well as detailed updates about the esrog orchards and the inspection process in Italy.

This is the story of how my grandfather and father worked tirelessly to secure kosher esrogim from Italy for the Frierdiker Rebbe and the Rebbe. Today, Altein Esrogim continues this tradition, providing these beautiful esrogim to chassidim around the world. My zeide would surely be proud to know that thousands of chayolim and their families now use Altein Esrogim while carrying out the Rebbe’s mivtzoim on the front lines.

Every year on Yud- Gimmel Tishrei, before the Rebbe’s farbrengen, long tables were arranged in Gan Eden HaTachton, the room next to the Rebbe’s room. My father would bring a suitcase filled with our finest esrogim and carefully arrange them on the tables. The Rebbe would then select one for himself and additional esrogim for leading shluchim spending Tishrei with him.

Be sure to order your very own Yanover esrog and lulav by 27 Elul for Sukkos!

And don’t forget to shake with other Yidden too!
